analysis.one_liner: Bars health insurers and employers from discriminating against people based on their genetic information.
analysis.headline: Despite 243 cosponsors — a majority of the House — the genetic discrimination ban never received a vote and died in House subcommittees.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it illegal for health insurers and employer health plans to deny coverage, raise premiums, or adjust group rates based on a person's genetic test results or family medical history. It would also have made it an unlawful employment practice to hire, fire, or assign work based on genetic information, and would have barred insurers and employers from demanding genetic tests or buying genetic data. People could still sue, and insurers could face civil penalties up to $50,000 for a first violation.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who has taken or may take a genetic test, or who has a family history of disease such as breast cancer, Huntington's, or sickle cell anemia. Today, a genetic test result could be used by an insurer to deny or price coverage, or by an employer in hiring and firing decisions. The bill would remove the fear that learning about your own DNA could cost you your health insurance or your job, and would likely make more people willing to get genetic testing that can catch disease early.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits health plans and insurers from denying eligibility or adjusting premiums for a group based on protected genetic information about a member of that group [S2].
Bars insurers in the individual market from setting enrollment rules or premium rates based on genetic information, and extends the same protections to Medicare supplemental (Medigap) policies [S3].

Makes it an unlawful employment practice for an employer, employment agency, labor organization, or training program to discriminate because of protected genetic information, and bars them from requesting or requiring genetic tests [S2].

Restricts collection and disclosure of genetic information, including bans on sharing it with employers, other insurers, or data services like the Medical Information Bureau, except with the person's prior written authorization [S3].

Gives individuals the right to sue in federal or state court, allows attorney's fees, and lets the government assess civil penalties of up to $50,000 for a first violation and $100,000 for repeat violations [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employers, who would lose the ability to use genetic test results and family history in pricing coverage or making hiring decisions, and would face compliance costs and civil penalties for violations. Insurers also warn that if high-risk people can buy coverage at standard rates, premiums for everyone in the pool rise.

drawbacks.text: The bill protects genetic information only. Insurers could still price coverage using an individual's current diagnosed health conditions, so a person already sick when applying for individual coverage would get no new protection — a limit critics of narrower bills pointed out [S3].

Banning the use of genetic information in insurance pricing creates what insurers call adverse selection: people who learn from a test that they are high-risk would have an incentive to buy more coverage, while insurers cannot adjust rates to reflect it, which can push premiums up for everyone in the pool.

The bill imposes compliance obligations and penalty exposure on employers of all sizes, including up to $50,000 in civil penalties per first violation, and requires employers to segregate genetic information into confidential medical files with limited disclosure channels [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For most people the benefit is concrete: without a legal ban, the growing ability to read your own DNA is also a risk — a test result can follow you into an insurance or hiring decision. The main honest cost is pressure on insurance premiums if high-risk people buy coverage at standard rates, and some compliance burden on employers. The bill's biggest design gap is that it leaves current diagnosed illness fair game for insurers, so it protects people who carry risk but are not yet sick — exactly the people genetic testing identifies.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to three House committees, which passed pieces of it down to their health and labor subcommittees, and it sat there with no further action until that Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Rep. Louise Slaughter introduced the Genetic Nondiscrimination in Health Insurance and Employment Act in the House on May 1, 2003 [S1].
The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and the Workforce Committees on the day it was introduced [S5].
Within a month, each referral had been passed down to a subcommittee: Health (twice) and Employer-Employee Relations [S5].
242 members cosponsored the bill — 190 of 205 House Democrats, 51 of 226 House Republicans, and the House's one Independent [S4].
The action history ends with those subcommittee referrals; no committee vote, floor vote, or Senate action ever occurred before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employers came out ahead: they kept the ability to use genetic test results and family medical history in pricing and employment decisions, and faced no federal ban on collecting or sharing that information.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and employers, still free to use DNA

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan but lopsided: 93% of House Democrats (190 of 205) cosponsored versus 23% of House Republicans (51 of 226), and the committees and floor schedule were controlled by Republicans.

industries.note: The bill would bar insurers from denying coverage, setting enrollment rules, or adjusting premiums based on genetic test results and family history, in both group and individual markets, with civil penalties up to $100,000 for repeat violations [S3]. Their pricing power over people whose genes predict future illness is exactly what the bill removes.

Employers, employment agencies, and labor organizations could no longer hire, fire, or classify workers based on genetic information, or request genetic tests, except in narrow cases like workplace toxic-substance monitoring with the employee's written consent [S3].

industries.industry: Insurance data services such as the Medical Information Bureau
industries.note: The bill bans insurers and plans from disclosing protected genetic information to the Medical Information Bureau and similar services that compile insurance data on individuals [S3].

By removing the fear that a test result could cost someone their insurance or job, the bill would remove a major reason people decline genetic tests and counseling that can catch treatable disease early.
